questions.q: What is the first step in tackling a problem properly?
a: Break it down into smaller parts
Pick the quickest possible solution
Ask an expert what they would do
Wait until more information arrives
questions.why: Lesson 1 says that instead of jumping to solutions, you should first split the problem into aspects.

questions.q: Which tool does Watanabe recommend for breaking a problem down?
a: Decision trees
Mind maps
SWOT analysis
Gantt charts
questions.why: Lesson 1 recommends decision trees, marking each branch yes or no to see whether it is really part of the problem.

questions.q: What is the point of the analysis step?
a: To stop accepting statements at face value
To confirm the first explanation you found
To gather support for your existing opinion
To speed up the decision-making process
questions.why: Lesson 2 says analysis means never taking claims at face value, including your own, so you pause and reflect.

questions.q: How should you treat the solutions you settle on?
a: As hypotheses that could be proven wrong
As final answers once the data agrees
As temporary fixes until a better plan appears
As bets worth making without further testing
questions.why: Lesson 3 defines a hypothesis as a currently accepted statement that may later turn out to be wrong.

questions.q: Why is the hypothesis approach so useful when you feel stuck?
a: It lets you switch course quickly when something fails
It guarantees the first plan will work
It removes the need to gather any more data
It puts the responsibility on other people
questions.why: Lesson 3 says treating plans as hypotheses keeps you flexible, so a failure leads to a new path instead of despair.
